performance_tasks.brief:
(1) Which description fits an electrode in an electrolytic cell?
A. An ionic liquid carrying charge between electrodes
B. An ion moving through the conducting solution
C. A separator preventing products from mixing
D. A conductor contacting the electrolyte [1]

(2) Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
A. Its ions can move and carry charge
B. Electrons move freely through the liquid salt
C. Neutral sodium atoms carry the current
D. Melting removes the charges from the ions [1]

(3) Which process defines the anode in electrolysis?
A. Electron gain at the positive electrode
B. Electron gain at the negative electrode
C. Electron loss at the negative electrode
D. Electron loss at the positive electrode [1]

(4) Which arrangement is suitable for an electrolytic cell?
A. Touching immersed electrodes across a DC supply
B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply
C. Separated dry electrodes above the electrolyte
D. Separated immersed electrodes with no external connection [1]

(5) Which half-equation represents reduction of copper(II) ions?
A. Cu + 2e⁻ → Cu²⁺
B. Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
C. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu [1]

(6) Which products form from molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
B. Cathode: lead; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lead [1]

(7) Why does dilute sulfuric acid give twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume during electrolysis with inert electrodes, at equal gas conditions?
A. Hydrogen molecules have twice oxygen’s volume at equal moles
B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
C. The hydrogen electrode receives twice the current
D. Oxygen atoms carry twice as many hydrogen atoms [1]

(8) Which products form during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous hydrochloric acid with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine
B. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: chlorine; anode: hydrogen
D. Cathode: hydrogen chloride; anode: chlorine [1]

(9) A molten binary salt contains Li⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Which products are predicted with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
B. Cathode: lithium; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lithium [1]

(10) Which anode change occurs during electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 with copper electrodes?
A. Copper ions gain electrons there
B. Copper atoms gain two electrons
C. Copper atoms dissolve as Cu²⁺
D. Water oxidises instead of copper [1]

(11) Which is a use of electroplating?
A. Mixing metals into bulk alloys
B. Applying a decorative metal coating
C. Removing a metal by dissolution
D. Filtering out dissolved metal ions [1]

(12) Why is molten cryolite used with pure aluminium oxide in aluminium manufacture?
A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature
B. It reduces the oxide instead of electrical current
C. It supplies most of the extracted aluminium
D. It raises the oxide’s required operating temperature [1]

Distractor explanations: A: This describes the electrolyte, not an electrode. B: An ion is a charge carrier, not the external conductor. C: A separator is not the conductor transferring electrons at the electrolyte boundary. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 2: Correct option A (1). A. Its ions can move and carry charge. Melting releases ions from fixed lattice positions. Distractor explanations: B: Charge passes through molten salt by ions, not free electrons. C: The mobile carriers are charged ions, not neutral atoms. D: Melting frees ions to move; it does not remove their charges. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 3: Correct option D (1). D. Electron loss at the positive electrode. Oxidation, loss of electrons, occurs at the anode. Distractor explanations: A: The anode loses electrons; electron gain is reduction. B: This describes cathodic reduction. C: In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive, not negative. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 4: Correct option B (1). B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply. The external circuit and mobile ions provide a complete path through separated electrodes. Distractor explanations: A: Touching electrodes can short-circuit the supply. C: Electrodes must contact the electrolyte to transfer charge. D: Electrolysis requires an external source and complete circuit. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 5: Correct option D (1). D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu Copper ions gain two electrons, balancing charge. Distractor explanations: A: Adding electrons cannot produce a positive ion from a neutral atom; charge is unbalanced. B: Reduction consumes electrons; this places them on the wrong side. C: This is oxidation of copper, the reverse process. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 6: Correct option C (1). C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine. Pb²⁺ gains electrons and Br⁻ loses electrons. Distractor explanations: A: The molten salt contains no water or hydrogen ions to produce hydrogen. B: The molten bromide supplies bromide ions, not an oxygen source. D: Lead forms at the cathode and bromine at the anode; these are reversed. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 7: Correct option B (1). B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. The balanced overall equation gives a 2:1 gas amount ratio. Distractor explanations: A: Equal gas amounts occupy equal volumes at the same conditions. C: The same current passes through both electrodes in the circuit. D: The volume ratio follows the balanced reaction, not this atomic description. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 8: Correct option A (1). A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine. Hydrogen ions gain electrons and chloride ions lose electrons under these conditions. Distractor explanations: B: Concentrated chloride solution produces chlorine at the inert anode under the stated conditions. C: This reverses the cathode and anode products. D: Hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen, not hydrogen chloride. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 9: Correct option C (1). C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine. Apply cation reduction and anion oxidation to the specified water-free melt. Distractor explanations: A: There is no water or hydrogen source in the specified molten salt. B: There is no oxygen-containing ion in the binary salt. D: Lithium is reduced at the cathode; bromide is oxidised at the anode. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 10: Correct option C (1). C. Copper atoms dissolve as Cu²⁺. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. This applies to an active copper anode. Distractor explanations: A: Copper ions gain electrons at the cathode, not the anode. B: Copper atoms lose electrons at the anode. D: An active copper anode dissolves instead of the inert-anode water-oxidation route. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 11: Correct option B (1). B. Applying a decorative metal coating. Electroplating deposits a metal coating on a conducting object. Distractor explanations: A: Bulk alloy formation is not deposition of a surface coating. C: Electroplating deposits metal on an object rather than simply removing it. D: Dissolved ions pass through ordinary filters; electroplating uses electrode reduction. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 12: Correct option A (1). A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature. The conducting molten mixture permits electrolysis at a lower temperature. Distractor explanations: B: Electrical reduction still releases the aluminium; cryolite is not the reducing agent. C: The aluminium oxide feed supplies the extracted metal. D: Cryolite lowers the required operating temperature rather than raising it. No mark for more than one selected option.
